Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Acute, profuse watery diarrhea with crampy abdominal pain for ~3 days; associated nausea/vomiting and feverish feeling.
- Trigger/exposure: No clear food exposure identified; household cluster with brother having similar illness.
- Symptom timeline/progression: Onset ~3 days ago (Mon/Tue); diarrhea has been frequent (roughly every hour while awake); crampy pain that comes and goes; vomiting occurs, notably after dairy exposure (milk triggering vomiting); feverish sensation; decreased urinary frequency; fluids “go straight through.”
- ENT symptoms: Felt hoarse (voice-related symptom reported by patient).
- Past medical history: Generally fit and well; no regular medications; no known drug allergies.
- Allergies: Not documented.
- Medications: Occasional paracetamol; not on regular meds; dosing/frequency not documented.
- Social history: Lives with sister and mother; smokes socially; tolerates alcohol socially; works in an office in Central London (government).
- Family history: Father with colon cancer (advanced stage); brother with similar illness; no known GI inflammatory or other ENT conditions.
- Accompaniment: Not specified; patient appeared to be managing symptoms at home.
- Other: Not awake to record vitals; no prior hospital/ED encounters noted.

Objective:
- Swelling/visible distribution: Not described.
- Airway/breathing: Not described.
- Mental status: Not described.
- Vitals/exam findings: Not recorded.
- Other observations: Patient reports feverish feeling; no observed anaphylaxis signs; no abdominal exam details provided.
- Presence of another person with patient: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration risk.
- Evidence from transcript: Onset ~3 days ago; profuse watery diarrhea with cramping; nausea/vomiting (milk-triggered); feverish feeling; high stool frequency; adequate but labile fluid intake; brother with similar illness suggests contagion; no blood in stool reported.
- DDx context (top items most aligned with transcript):
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis (high likelihood): Classic presentation in young adult; household transmission plausible; symptoms align with viral gastroenteritis.
    - Supporting: abrupt onset ~3 days ago; watery diarrhea; crampy pain; nausea/vomiting; feverish sensation; family cluster.
    - Opposing: No vitals provided; no stool testing done to confirm.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis / foodborne infection (medium): Plausible given duration and systemic symptoms; household exposure possible.
    - Supporting: Several days of diarrhea with cramps and fever.
    - Opposing: No blood in stool; no explicit food exposure identified.
  - Lactose intolerance / post-infectious lactose malabsorption (medium): Dairy-triggered vomiting noted; could contribute to symptoms.
    - Supporting: Vomiting after milk; crampy diarrhea.
    - Opposing: Diarrhea occurs with various foods; systemic symptoms present.
- Conflict: None noted between transcript and DDx; aligned with gastroenteritis framework.

Plan:
- Immediate actions/therapeutic:
  - Advise oral rehydration with Diarolyte or equivalent oral rehydration solution; emphasize hydration due to high stool frequency.
  - Continue paracetamol as needed for fever/pain; avoid alcohol.
  - Begin clear fluids and soft diet (e.g., soups, mashed foods); gradually advance diet as tolerated.
- Patient/caregiver instructions:
  - Stay hydrated; use ORS regularly; monitor urine output.
  - If unable to keep fluids down or signs of dehydration develop, seek medical attention promptly.
  - Return if persistent vomiting, high fever, blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, or worsening symptoms.
  - Consider dairy management if lactose-intolerant symptoms suspected; dairy temporarily limited if symptoms worsen.
- Red flags / escalation criteria:
  - Signs of dehydration (dry mouth, reduced urine, dizziness), persistent high fever, inability to keep fluids down, or blood in stool.
- Follow-up:
  - Recheck by phone or clinic in 1–2 days or sooner if symptoms worsen; seek in-person assessment if dehydration or bowel symptoms persist beyond 48 hours.
  - No ENT/allergy specific referrals indicated at this time; educate on self-care and hydration.
- COVID-19 vaccine suitability: Not discussed; no action indicated.
- Additional notes: No imaging or labs ordered at this time given clinical impression of self-limited gastroenteritis.

Document quality:
- Missing elements clinically expected for acute GI presentation:
  - Allergy list (documented as none known).
  - Prior anaphylaxis plan and auto-injector availability (not applicable here; not documented).
  - Immunization history relevant to GI pathogens (not documented).
  - Objective vitals (BP, HR, temp) and physical abdominal exam findings (not recorded).
  - Stool testing, dehydration assessment metrics, or stool culture results (not performed).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Sufficient for clinical synthesis; no major ambiguities; vitals/exam not recorded.

Note: The DDx supports the impression of acute gastroenteritis, with viral gastroenteritis being the most likely diagnosis given the presentation and household exposure. Bacterial gastroenteritis remains a reasonable consideration; lactose intolerance/malabsorption could contribute to symptoms, especially with dairy-triggered vomiting. No conflicting evidence identified within the transcript.

End of note.
